input: When we make a measurement of any kind, it is very important to understand that the value we read off an instrument is never going to be perfectly exact, and this is where the closely related but subtly different concepts of error and uncertainty come into play. In this passage, we are going to explore the ideas of absolute error and relative error by looking at a simple temperature measurement. The absolute error is essentially the size of the difference between the measured value and the true value, and it is expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error, on the other hand, expresses that same difference as a fraction or percentage of the reading, which can often be more informative. Let us consider a concrete example: suppose we have a temperature reading of 180 units, and suppose the tolerance on that reading is 0.5% of the reading itself. Working through the calculation, 0.5% of 180 units gives us an absolute error of 0.9 units, which tells us the scale of the discrepancy in the units we are actually working with. It is worth emphasising that error and uncertainty are not really the same thing, even though people often use the words interchangeably: error refers to a difference in a particular measurement, whereas uncertainty describes the doubt or spread that surrounds a result more generally, and carefully distinguishing between these two ideas is an important part of reporting measurements in a clear and rigorous way. In short, the relative error here is 0.5%, the absolute error is 0.9 units, and stating the tolerance as 0.5% of the reading is what connects the two statements.
target: Absolute error is the size of the difference between a reading and the value the reading stands for, stated in the units of the reading. Relative error is the same difference stated as a fraction of the reading, usually as a percentage. A temperature measurement shows the two forms on one set of figures. The reading is 180 units and the tolerance is 0.5% of the reading. The absolute error is thus 0.5% of 180 units, which is 0.9 units. The relative error is the tolerance itself, 0.5%, and it carries no unit. The two statements answer different questions. The absolute error (0.9 units) gives the size of the discrepancy in the units of the measurement, and the relative error (0.5%) gives that size against the size of the reading. Error and uncertainty are separate terms and are not merged here. Error belongs to a single reading: it is the difference between that reading and the value it stands for, and it can in principle be stated as one number. Uncertainty belongs to the result: it states the range within which the value is held to lie, and it reflects what is not known about the measurement rather than a counted difference. A report that gives an error where an uncertainty is meant overstates what the measurement establishes, and a report that gives an uncertainty as an error does the same in the other direction.
